top.title: Ancient Siberian tomb reveals surprising secrets of cannabis use 2,800 years ago
top.summary: Scientists investigating a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb discovered roughly 1,000 cannabis seeds and chemical evidence suggesting ancient Scythians used the plant for its intoxicating effects. The remarkable find, surrounded by evidence of elaborate burial rituals and animal sacrifices, offers the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence of psychoactive cannabis use.
top.text: A remarkable discovery in a nearly 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb has provided the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence that people used cannabis for its intoxicating effects. By examining ancient cannabis seeds and chemical traces preserved in human hair, researchers have uncovered new clues about the role of the plant in prehistoric burial rituals. Cannabis is among the most widely used psychoactive plants in the modern world, but tracing its use thousands of years into the past presents a major archaeological challenge. Flowers, leaves, and resins tend to decompose over time, leaving little physical evidence behind. Ancient communities also relied on cannabis for practical purposes, including producing fiber and oil, making it difficult to distinguish these uses from medicinal or recreational consumption. An international team led by Dr. Gino Caspari, affiliated with the Institute of Archaeological Sciences at the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, investigated an elaborate tomb in the Republic of Tyva in southern Siberia. The burial site belonged to prominent members of the Scythians, a culture known for its skilled horseback riders who inhabited the vast Eurasian steppe. During the investigation, researchers recovered approximately 1,000 cannabis seeds from the tomb. They used radiocarbon dating to determine the age of six individual seeds. Combined with other dating evidence, the results indicate that the seeds were deposited in the burial site during the early eighth century B.C. "The seeds show that cannabis played an important role in the rituals surrounding the burial," says Caspari, an archaeologist and the study's lead author. The researchers also analyzed human hair preserved in the tomb's central burial chamber. Chemical evidence in several samples pointed to cannabis consumption, providing a crucial connection between the plant remains and the people buried at the site. "This study is particularly insightful because it combines the analysis of plant remains with molecular traces in the human body," says Caspari. Although the cannabis seeds were remarkably well preserved, their presence alone could not establish whether the plant was used for its mind-altering effects. The seeds probably came from wild cannabis plants, and researchers could not determine whether people had deliberately cultivated them for their psychoactive properties. The strongest evidence came from the preserved human hair. Using high-resolution mass spectrometry and other analytical techniques, the team identified clear chemical signals consistent with cannabinol (CBN) in several samples. CBN can form when tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary compound responsible for cannabis intoxication, undergoes oxidation. The researchers also detected weaker signals that matched the mass of THC, further supporting the possibility that the individuals had consumed cannabis. While these chemical findings indicate cannabis use, they cannot reveal how much was consumed or exactly how the compounds entered the body. The individuals may have inhaled cannabis smoke or consumed the plant in another way, but the available evidence cannot establish a particular method. Other archaeological discoveries from later periods in Central Asia provide clearer evidence of cannabis inhalation. At those sites, researchers have identified cannabinoid residues on heated stones and inside vessels, pointing to the use of heat to release compounds that could be inhaled. "The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties," says Caspari, who conducts research at the Institute of Archaeological Sciences at the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute for Geoanthropology in Jena (Germany). The cannabis evidence was discovered within an elaborate ceremonial burial site, suggesting that the plant may have been connected to important Scythian funerary traditions. "In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well," says Gino Caspari. Earlier research at the site identified the remains of 18 horses that had been deliberately positioned on the burial mound. Continued excavations have since uncovered evidence of several dozen more sacrificed horses, along with scattered human bones. These discoveries reveal the extraordinary scale of the burial ceremonies and provide important context for understanding why cannabis may have been included among the materials deposited in the tomb. Taken together, the seeds and chemical traces in human hair represent the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence currently known for cannabis use associated with intoxication. However, several questions remain unanswered. The researchers cannot determine how much THC the ancient cannabis contained, whether the plants were particularly potent, or whether Scythian communities had begun deliberately selecting or cultivating cannabis varieties with higher concentrations of psychoactive compounds. To investigate these questions, the team is now studying genetic material recovered from the ancient plant remains. The unusually good preservation of the cannabis DNA could provide valuable insights into how humans domesticated the plant and how it spread across different regions over thousands of years. "We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples," says Gino Caspari. "DNA preservation is excellent in this case. This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of this crop soon." Materials provided by University of Bern . Note: Content may be edited for style and length. top.title: Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk
top.summary: A surprising new study suggests that a stronger flu shot could offer older adults significantly greater protection against Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at UTHealth Houston analyzed nearly 200,000 adults ages 65 and older and found that those who received a high-dose influenza vaccine had a nearly 55% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's, compared with a 40% reduction previously associated with the standard-dose vaccine.
top.text: A higher dose of the annual flu vaccine may offer older adults an unexpected benefit: a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. In a large study led by researchers at UTHealth Houston, adults ages 65 and older who received a high-dose influenza vaccine were less likely to develop Alzheimer's than those given the standard-dose version. The findings, published in the medical journal Neurology , suggest that the strength of a flu vaccine could matter for more than just protection against influenza. The discovery grew out of an unexpected conversation between a UTHealth Houston physician and local public health officials. What began as a visit to discuss earlier vaccine research eventually led scientists to investigate whether different flu vaccine doses might be associated with different levels of Alzheimer's risk. Alzheimer's disease is the leading cause of dementia and an increasingly serious public health concern. In 2025, more than 7 million Americans ages 65 and older were living with the disease, representing approximately 1 in 9 people in that age group. That figure is projected to more than double by 2050. Researchers have been exploring whether common vaccines might influence the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's. In a 2022 study , a team led by Paul Schulz, MD, found that flu vaccination was associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's among adults 65 and older. Schulz is a professor of neurology at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston and director of the Neurocognitive Disorders Center at UTHealth Houston Neurosciences. Three years after that earlier investigation, Schulz and his colleagues published new research examining a more specific question: Could receiving a stronger flu vaccine be associated with an even greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk? The idea came from public health officials who had learned about the team's previous findings and invited Schulz to discuss them. "The public health department had seen our vaccine research and asked if I could come down to talk to them about it," said Schulz, who is the senior author of the study and the Rick McCord Professor in Neurology and Umphrey Family Professor in Neurodegenerative Diseases at McGovern Medical School. "We went through the findings, and they asked if there was a difference with different dosages; I was confused." As people grow older, their immune systems gradually become less effective at recognizing and fighting infections. This age-related decline can make influenza particularly dangerous for seniors. To help address that vulnerability, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends high-dose influenza vaccines as a preferred option for adults ages 65 and older. These vaccines contain four times as much influenza antigen as standard-dose shots. Antigens are the components of a vaccine that stimulate the immune system to recognize and defend against a virus. The higher dose is designed to produce a stronger immune response in older adults, whose immune systems may respond less effectively to conventional vaccines. Schulz had not previously realized that this stronger formulation was available. "I was stunned that, as a physician, I didn't know a higher dose was offered," Schulz said. Annual flu vaccination is recommended broadly, but preventing influenza is especially important for people with Alzheimer's disease. Flu infections and their complications can pose serious health risks for individuals already coping with cognitive impairment. Before 2022, the CDC did not express a preference for one type of injectable influenza vaccine over another for people ages 65 and older. Instead, the guidance emphasized receiving a flu shot every year, regardless of the specific formulation. Previous research from UTHealth Houston had already linked inactivated influenza vaccines, which use viruses that cannot cause influenza infection, to a 40% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. However, researchers had not yet determined whether a higher vaccine dose might be associated with additional benefits. Another practical issue made the question particularly relevant. As the population of older Americans continues to grow, demand for high-dose flu vaccines sometimes exceeds the available supply. Consequently, some seniors receive standard-dose vaccines instead. This variation gave researchers an opportunity to compare Alzheimer's outcomes among older adults who had received different formulations. "So we started looking, and sure enough, we were able to put together thousands and thousands of people over the age of 65 who got the high- or low-dose vaccine. They're more at risk for Alzheimer's than anybody else, of course, because it's age-related and we could look at high-dose versus low-dose and see if there was a difference," Schulz said. To investigate the potential connection, the research team analyzed data from nearly 200,000 men and women ages 65 and older. The results showed that people who received high-dose influenza vaccines had a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease than those who received the standard-dose formulation. The researchers reported that standard-dose influenza vaccination was associated with a 40% reduction in Alzheimer's risk, while high-dose vaccination was linked to a reduction of nearly 55%. The association was particularly pronounced among women, who appeared to experience a greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk with the stronger vaccine. These findings add to growing evidence of a possible relationship between influenza vaccination and brain health. They also raise important questions about whether the immune response triggered by vaccination might influence biological processes involved in Alzheimer's disease. However, the findings demonstrate an association rather than establishing cause and effect. Additional research is needed to determine whether high-dose flu vaccination directly reduces the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's and to understand the mechanisms that might explain the connection. With Alzheimer's affecting millions of Americans and the number of cases expected to rise sharply in the coming decades, researchers are searching for practical ways to reduce risk. The possibility that an existing vaccine could have benefits extending beyond influenza prevention is particularly intriguing. Unlike an entirely new treatment, flu vaccination is already widely used, and higher-dose formulations are specifically designed for older adults. The new findings suggest that vaccine dosage could be an important consideration in future studies exploring the relationship between the immune system and Alzheimer's disease. For now, the research provides another reason to investigate the potential benefits of influenza vaccination while emphasizing the need for further studies before drawing conclusions about Alzheimer's prevention. Avram Samuel Bukhbinder, MD, a graduate of McGovern Medical School who is currently a clinical fellow in neurology at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard University, served as a corresponding author of the study. Schulz is also a faculty member of The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center UTHealth Houston Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences. Other contributors from McGovern Medical School included Elizabeth He, visiting scholar in the Department of Neurology; Kristofer Harris, MPH, research coordinator in the Department of Neurology; Mya Rodriguez, graduate research assistant in the Department of Neurology; Kamal Phelps, MD, an alumnus of the Department of Neurology; Jenna Thomas; Gabriela Cruz, MD, resident in the Department of Neurology; and Lauren Jhin. top.title: An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin
top.summary: A surprising new study suggests that an anti-aging drug could help protect people genetically predisposed to Alzheimer's disease. Researchers found that just four weeks of low-dose rapamycin improved brain blood flow in healthy middle-aged adults carrying the high-risk APOE4 gene variant, with women showing the strongest benefits. Because declining blood flow can occur years before Alzheimer's symptoms appear, the discovery raises hopes for preventing or delaying the disease before memory loss begins.
top.text: A drug commonly used to prevent organ transplant rejection may offer an unexpected new approach to protecting people at increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at the University of Missouri have discovered that rapamycin, a medication also studied for its effects on aging, can improve blood flow in the brains of middle-aged adults who carry a gene variant linked to Alzheimer's. The findings could help scientists develop strategies to address Alzheimer's risk long before memory problems appear. The research also adds to the University of Missouri's growing contributions to understanding and potentially preventing the most common form of dementia. The study was led by Ai-Ling Lin, a professor in the university's School of Medicine and an investigator at the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building. Her work focuses on identifying changes in the brain that occur before Alzheimer's symptoms develop and finding ways to intervene early. A major focus of Lin's research is the APOE4 gene variant, which is associated with a substantially increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease later in life. People who carry APOE4 can experience reduced blood flow in certain areas of the brain years before they begin having noticeable memory difficulties. Because these circulation changes can occur so early, researchers believe they could provide an important warning sign of increased Alzheimer's risk. Lin's latest findings suggest that improving brain circulation with an existing medication may be one way to address these early changes. "Alzheimer's tends to happen more in older people, especially for those with APOE4," Lin said. "If we can slow down aging in the brain for those people most at risk, maybe we can reduce the risk of them developing Alzheimer's disease." Rapamycin is already used in medicine to prevent the immune system from rejecting transplanted organs and to treat certain rare conditions. However, researchers have also been investigating its potential to slow biological aging and protect the brain. Before joining the University of Missouri, Lin conducted experiments involving mice that carried APOE4. Her earlier research showed that rapamycin could slow brain aging and increase blood flow in these animals. Those results prompted an important question: Could rapamycin produce similar benefits in people who have a genetic predisposition to Alzheimer's but have not yet developed the disease? To investigate, Lin studied healthy adults between the ages of 45 and 65, including people who carried APOE4 and others who did not. All participants received a low daily dose of rapamycin for four weeks. When researchers examined the results, they found a notable difference between the two groups. Brain blood flow improved among participants carrying APOE4, but the same benefit was not observed in those without the gene variant. This suggests that rapamycin may have particular potential for people whose genetics place them at greater risk of Alzheimer's. Although the study did not establish whether the treatment could prevent Alzheimer's or preserve memory over time, the improved circulation offers a promising direction for future research. Women With the Alzheimer's Risk Gene Saw the Greatest Benefits Another intriguing finding emerged when the researchers examined differences between male and female participants. Women carrying APOE4 experienced the largest improvements in brain blood flow following treatment. That result may be especially important because women account for nearly two-thirds of people living with Alzheimer's disease. "We also found that females with APOE4 saw the greatest improvement in brain blood flow, which is significant given that nearly two-thirds of people with Alzheimer's are women," she said. "This research is an example of precision medicine, as we work to identify who can benefit from this drug the most." The results highlight the potential of precision medicine, an approach that considers individual characteristics, including genetics, when determining which treatments may be most effective. Rather than assuming that a medication will benefit everyone equally, researchers hope to identify the people most likely to respond. Lin, who is also a professor in the university's College of Arts and Science, credits Mizzou's collaborative research environment with helping advance discoveries like these. At the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building, scientists and medical professionals work together in the same facility. This collaboration is designed to help move promising laboratory findings into human clinical studies more quickly. The latest results provide an encouraging starting point for investigating whether rapamycin could eventually help delay or reduce Alzheimer's risk in genetically vulnerable individuals. More research will be needed to determine whether the changes in brain blood flow lead to lasting improvements in brain health or a lower likelihood of developing the disease. The study, "EXPRESS: Rapamycin increases cerebral blood flow and modulates metabolic, inflammatory, and microbiome profiles in healthy middle-aged APOE4 carriers: a pilot single-arm trial" was published in Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism . top.title: Magic mushrooms rewire the brain in a way scientists didn't expect
top.summary: A surprising discovery reveals how psilocybin, the active compound in magic mushrooms, rapidly reshapes the brain by creating new neural connections and strengthening them. Researchers found that the drug behaves differently in healthy and chronically stressed mice, potentially helping repair brain circuits damaged by prolonged stress. Most intriguingly, they identified a way to trigger this brain rewiring without the behavioral response associated with psychedelic effects.
top.text: A new study from the University of California, Santa Cruz, has revealed how psilocybin, the psychedelic substance found in "magic mushrooms," changes the brain by reorganizing connections between nerve cells. The findings could eventually help scientists develop treatments for mental health conditions that capture some of psilocybin's potential benefits without producing hallucinations. The research, published October 15 in Nature Neuroscience , found that psilocybin rapidly encourages brain cells to form new connections and helps those connections mature. At the same time, it promotes the removal of certain older connections, suggesting that its effects involve more than simply increasing communication between neurons. Experiments in mice also revealed something especially intriguing. The researchers were able to separate the cellular changes responsible for this rewiring from a behavioral response commonly associated with psychedelic effects. This suggests that some of psilocybin's effects on brain structure may be achievable without the hallucinations typically associated with the drug. The discovery could provide a foundation for developing medications that enhance the brain's ability to adapt and reorganize itself, a property known as neuroplasticity. Such treatments might eventually offer new approaches for depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and other psychiatric conditions. The team also identified a particular group of neurons in the cerebral cortex that plays an essential role in psilocybin's effects on brain connections. Importantly, the researchers discovered that the drug does not affect every brain in the same way. Its influence depends partly on whether the brain has previously experienced chronic stress. "I consider this work a major advance, particularly in our understanding of how psilocybin reshapes neural circuits and its potential implications for treating mental disorders," said senior author Yi Zuo, professor of molecular, cell, and developmental biology at UC Santa Cruz. Scientific interest in psychedelic drugs has changed dramatically over the past century. During the middle of the 20th century, substances such as psilocybin and LSD attracted attention from Western researchers because of their powerful effects on perception, consciousness, and mood. Early studies suggested these compounds might have applications in psychiatric treatment. However, scientific investigations slowed substantially after the United States passed the Controlled Substances Act in 1970, which imposed strict restrictions on these substances. In recent years, researchers have renewed their interest in psychedelics, particularly their ability to produce rapid and potentially lasting changes in brain function. Scientists sometimes describe these compounds as "psychoplastogens" because they can stimulate neuroplasticity after a single dose. Neuroplasticity refers to the brain's capacity to change its structure and activity by forming, strengthening, reorganizing, or removing connections between neurons. This property is particularly interesting for mental health treatment because conditions such as depression can involve disruptions in the circuits responsible for regulating mood, emotions, and behavior. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has previously recognized the therapeutic potential of psychedelic research by granting Breakthrough Therapy designations to substances including psilocybin and MDMA. These designations are intended to accelerate the development and review of promising treatments for serious medical conditions. In September 2026, the FDA took another step toward evaluating psychedelic treatments by organizing a public hearing titled "Considerations for Potential Future Therapeutic Use of Psychedelic Drugs." Experts discussed how healthcare professionals administering psychedelic treatments should be qualified, how potential risks could be managed through Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) programs, and how future clinical trials should be designed. As regulators examine ways psychedelic treatments might eventually become part of mainstream healthcare, researchers are increasingly focused on understanding exactly what these substances do to the brain. Identifying the cellular mechanisms behind their effects could help scientists develop treatments that are both effective and safer to administer. To investigate how psilocybin changes brain structure, the UC Santa Cruz team used an advanced imaging method called two-photon microscopy. This technology allows scientists to observe extremely small structures inside living tissue with remarkable detail. Using it, the researchers followed individual connections on neurons in living mice over several weeks, allowing them to see how those structures changed after psilocybin treatment. Their attention centered on tiny projections called dendritic spines. These structures extend from neurons and receive messages from neighboring nerve cells. They help form synapses, the specialized junctions through which neurons communicate. Synapses are essential for processing information and supporting functions such as learning, memory, and emotional regulation. Changes in their number, strength, and organization can alter the way information travels through the brain. Within just 24 hours of psilocybin administration, the researchers observed a substantial increase in newly forming dendritic spines. But the drug did more than encourage new connections to appear. It also helped them develop into more mature structures at an unusually rapid pace. Normally, newly formed spines often begin as small, immature structures described as "stubby." Many remain unstable and disappear before becoming fully developed connections. After psilocybin treatment, however, a much larger proportion developed into structures with a distinctive "mushroom" appearance. These mature spines are generally more stable and contain higher concentrations of receptors that receive chemical signals from neighboring neurons. Because of these features, mature spines can support stronger and more persistent communication between brain cells, potentially contributing to lasting changes in circuits involved in memory and mood. For lead author Jacob Baker, one of the biggest questions is whether these structural changes require the intense psychedelic experience typically produced by psilocybin. "Psychedelics are fascinating compounds because they have the potential to profoundly transform who we are by reshaping the neural circuits in our brains," said Baker, a Ph.D. student in Zuo's lab. "These newly formed connections can integrate into existing neural circuitry and persist over time, leaving a lasting structural trace of psilocybin's effects on the brain." One of the study's most revealing findings was that psilocybin's influence on brain connections changed depending on whether the mice had experienced prolonged stress. In healthy mice, psilocybin initially stimulated the formation of new dendritic spines. Over the following three weeks, however, the number of connections gradually moved back toward its previous level. This happened partly because the brain eliminated some connections that had existed before treatment. Rather than simply accumulating additional synapses, the healthy brain appeared to reorganize its existing circuitry while maintaining an overall balance. The researchers observed a different response in mice exposed to chronic stress. top.title: Scientists discover a hidden driver of high cholesterol and a way to stop it
top.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden mechanism that allows high-cholesterol diets to undermine the body's natural cholesterol defenses, and blocking it dramatically lowered harmful LDL cholesterol in mice. Even more promising, an experimental drug targeting this pathway has already passed an early human safety trial, potentially speeding the development of a new treatment for high cholesterol.
top.text: Heart disease linked to high cholesterol continues to be the leading cause of death worldwide. Although doctors have more treatment options than ever, many people still struggle to lower their cholesterol to safe levels. Others experience side effects that make existing medications difficult to take. Researchers at the University of California San Diego School of Medicine have now identified a previously unknown biological pathway that helps explain why diets high in cholesterol can gradually weaken the body's ability to remove harmful low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol from the bloodstream. Even more promising, they have identified an experimental drug that has already undergone safety testing in humans and could potentially interfere with this process. The findings, published in Nature , could open the door to a new approach to treating high cholesterol. "We've known for a long time that a high-cholesterol diet reduces the liver's ability to clear cholesterol from the blood, but we didn't fully understand why," said senior author Alan Saltiel, PhD, professor of medicine at UC San Diego School of Medicine and director of the UC San Diego/UCLA Diabetes Research Center. "This new discovery explains a critical piece of that puzzle." The liver plays a central role in controlling cholesterol levels. It removes cholesterol from the bloodstream so it can be processed, broken down, and used by other parts of the body. To accomplish this, liver cells rely on structures called LDL receptors. Located on the surface of these cells, the receptors work much like docking stations, capturing LDL cholesterol circulating in the blood and bringing it inside for processing. The number of available receptors matters. When liver cells have more LDL receptors, they can remove more cholesterol from circulation. This is one reason widely used cholesterol medications, including statins and PCSK9 inhibitors, are effective. They help maintain or increase the number of receptors available to clear LDL cholesterol. Using experiments involving mice and human cells, the researchers discovered a previously unrecognized process that interferes with the liver's ability to clear cholesterol. Over time, this mechanism reduces the number of LDL receptors, making it harder for the body to keep blood cholesterol under control. The process begins with a protein known as Ral, which Saltiel had previously investigated in fat cells. The team discovered that consuming high amounts of dietary cholesterol activates Ral, setting off a chain of events that leads to the loss of LDL receptors. As Ral activity increases, fewer receptors remain available to remove harmful cholesterol from the bloodstream. The researchers then identified another critical piece of the mechanism: an enzyme called cathepsin A (CTSA). This enzyme helps drive the process responsible for depleting LDL receptors. When scientists used a small molecule inhibitor to block CTSA, the results were striking. LDL receptors became more stable, and levels of circulating LDL cholesterol dropped dramatically in mice. The discovery is especially significant because the newly identified pathway is different from those targeted by current cholesterol medications. That distinction could make it possible to develop treatments for patients who do not respond adequately to existing drugs. "There's still a real need for new cholesterol-lowering options, since some people can't get to safe levels even with the drugs we have now," said Saltiel. "This new pathway we discovered is completely separate from anything that existing drugs target, so it gives us a new opportunity to fill that gap." Discovering a new biological target is usually only the beginning of a lengthy drug development process. Researchers often need years of additional work to identify a suitable compound and determine whether it can be used safely in people. In this case, however, the scientists may already have a promising candidate. A drug designed to inhibit CTSA had previously been developed as a potential treatment for heart failure. Although the program was eventually discontinued for strategic reasons, the experimental medication had already progressed through a Phase 1 clinical trial, where it was successfully evaluated for safety in humans. That earlier work could provide an important advantage. Rather than beginning drug development from scratch, researchers believe the existing CTSA inhibitor may be ready to advance into a Phase 2 clinical trial to investigate its effectiveness against high cholesterol. The findings are still at an early stage, and the drug has not yet been shown to lower cholesterol in humans. Nevertheless, its previous clinical testing could shorten the path toward determining whether this new treatment strategy works in patients. "Luckily, there's an experimental drug sitting on the shelf that's already been shown to be safe in humans," said Saltiel. "We hope to test whether this might be effective by conducting a clinical trial -- which could potentially bring a new treatment option to patients much sooner than would have been expected." top.title: Scientists find surprisingly little evidence that medical cannabis helps you sleep
top.summary: A major new review challenges the growing enthusiasm for medical cannabis as an insomnia treatment, finding little reliable evidence that it improves sleep quality, sleep duration, or daytime functioning. Researchers caution that this doesn't mean cannabis is ineffective, only that existing studies are too weak to establish whether it works.
top.text: A major new scientific review is raising questions about whether medical cannabis actually helps people with insomnia. Despite growing interest in cannabis as a sleep treatment, researchers found that the available evidence is too weak to reliably determine whether it improves sleep quality, sleep duration, or how well people function during the day. Insomnia affects millions of people and can make it difficult to fall asleep, remain asleep throughout the night, or wake up feeling rested. Beyond the frustration of sleepless nights, the condition can seriously disrupt daily life and increase the likelihood of developing anxiety or depression. Treatments for insomnia include cognitive behavioral therapy, which helps people change thoughts and habits that interfere with sleep, as well as medications such as antidepressants and antipsychotics. However, these approaches do not work equally well for everyone, fueling interest in alternative options. Medical cannabis has attracted particular attention because of its potential to improve sleep. Unlike recreational cannabis, regulated medical products typically contain carefully measured amounts of THC and CBD, two compounds found in cannabis, and are administered as tablets, sprays, or oils. Despite its growing popularity, scientists have continued to debate whether cannabis offers meaningful benefits for people with insomnia. To investigate, researchers from The Cochrane Associate Centre at the Universidad Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires and the University of Manitoba examined nine clinical studies involving 537 adults between the ages of 18 and 76 who were receiving treatment for insomnia. Most of the studies involved people with primary insomnia, meaning their sleep problems were not attributed to another medical condition. Eight trials compared regulated medical cannabis with a placebo, an inactive treatment used to measure whether a therapy produces genuine benefits. The remaining trial compared cannabis with amitriptyline, an antidepressant that is sometimes used to treat sleep problems. Across the placebo comparisons, medical cannabis produced little or no clinically meaningful improvement in sleep quality, satisfaction with sleep, total hours slept, or daytime functioning. The researchers also identified potential drawbacks. Participants who received medical cannabis were substantially more likely to experience mild side effects, including dizziness and dry mouth, than those given a placebo. However, this finding came from a relatively small number of studies, limiting confidence in the result. There was some indication that medical cannabis might improve overall quality of life. Yet the evidence supporting this possibility was highly uncertain. When the findings were combined, the results were consistent with outcomes ranging from a slight decline in quality of life to a substantial improvement. "The main message is that the research currently available is not sufficient to reliably answer whether medical cannabis helps people with insomnia," says Dr. Lucia Varela, lead author of the study from the University of Manitoba, Canada. "This does not mean that medical cannabis is ineffective. It means that, based on the evidence we have, we cannot draw reliable conclusions about its effectiveness for insomnia in the general population." One of the biggest problems was the quality of the research itself. The reviewers rated their confidence in the available evidence as low or very low, citing small study populations, conflicting findings, and potential bias in how the trials were conducted. Another challenge was the lack of consistency between studies. Researchers tested different medical cannabis products, making it difficult to directly compare their results or determine whether particular formulations might work better than others. The studies were also relatively short. The longest followed participants for just 12 weeks, leaving major unanswered questions about whether medical cannabis could provide lasting sleep benefits or produce additional effects with prolonged use. The researchers also cautioned that the study participants did not adequately represent the broader population of people living with insomnia. Women accounted for nearly three-quarters (72.66% of participants), and the research was heavily weighted toward younger adults. As a result, it remains unclear whether the findings would apply equally to men, older individuals, or people whose insomnia occurs alongside other medical conditions. Taken together, these limitations mean that the existing research cannot establish whether medical cannabis is an effective insomnia treatment. The authors emphasize that larger, more rigorous clinical trials are needed before it can be confidently recommended for improving sleep. Importantly, the findings do not establish that medical cannabis is ineffective. Instead, they highlight how much remains unknown about a treatment that has gained considerable attention despite limited high-quality evidence. "The evidence is too weak and uncertain to draw firm conclusions about the use of medical cannabis for insomnia," says Dr. Luis Garegnani, senior author from Universidad Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires, Argentina. "Rather than viewing the findings as either an endorsement or a rejection of medical cannabis, clinicians and patients should recognize the uncertainty and consider individual circumstances while better evidence is generated." top.title: 30,000-year-old DNA reveals Ice Age Europeans were far more connected than we thought
top.summary: Scientists have uncovered surprising DNA evidence that Europeans living more than 30,000 years ago were connected across vast distances, challenging the idea that ancient populations remained largely isolated. Genetic clues from human remains and cave sediments reveal prehistoric migration, long-lasting communities, and survival through the harshest conditions of the Ice Age.
top.text: More than 30,000 years ago, people living across Ice Age Europe were far more connected than scientists previously believed. New genetic evidence reveals unexpected links between populations separated by enormous distances, challenging the long-held idea that eastern and western European groups remained largely isolated from one another. An international research team led by the University of Vienna made the discovery by analyzing ancient DNA from rare human remains and traces of human genetic material preserved in cave sediments. Published in Science Advances , the findings provide a new picture of how prehistoric Europeans interacted, exchanged genes, and maintained populations through thousands of years of dramatic environmental change. The research focuses on people associated with one of Europe's major Paleolithic cultures (the Gravettian), which flourished across the continent roughly 34,000 to 25,000 years ago. Archaeological discoveries have long suggested that these ancient populations maintained connections over considerable distances. However, previous genetic evidence pointed to relatively distinct eastern and western ancestry groups. By combining new genetic findings with previously collected DNA, researchers uncovered evidence that these groups were more interconnected than expected. They also found signs that certain populations in southwestern Europe maintained their genetic ancestry for thousands of years. A Woman From 30,000 Years Ago Reveals Hidden Genetic Connections One of the most revealing discoveries came from the remains of a woman who lived approximately 30,000 years ago in what is now southwestern France. Found at Isturitz Cave, her remains provided the oldest genome-wide genetic dataset yet obtained from a modern human in southwestern Europe. Her DNA contained a surprising combination of ancestry. Although most of her genetic background was associated with western European populations, she also carried ancestry linked to people from central and eastern Europe. Using genetic modeling, researchers estimated that this mixing between populations occurred approximately 32,500 to 31,500 years ago. The finding suggests that genetic connections extended across large portions of Europe much earlier than scientists had previously established. "Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed," says first author Pere Gelabert, Department of Evolutionary Anthropology at the University of Vienna. "Gene flow across such large distances adds a new dimension to our understanding of how Gravettian populations were connected." The researchers identified a similar genetic signature in another ancient individual whose remains had previously been studied at Ormesson, France. Combined with archaeological discoveries, the evidence strengthens the possibility that Isturitz Cave served as a gathering place where different groups of prehistoric people encountered one another. Ancient DNA Hidden in Cave Sediments Reveals Ice Age Survival While some ancient Europeans exchanged genes across considerable distances, other populations appear to have maintained a continuous genetic presence in particular regions for thousands of years. Evidence from Chufín Cave in northern Spain suggests that ancestry associated with western European populations persisted in southwestern Europe over an extended period. The researchers also used an increasingly valuable technique that allows scientists to recover human DNA directly from cave sediments, even when no identifiable human remains are present. Tiny traces of genetic material left behind by ancient inhabitants can survive in soil and other deposits for thousands of years, providing information about people whose bones have never been found. At El Mirón Cave in Cantabria, Spain, the team recovered human nuclear DNA from a sediment layer dating back approximately 22,000 years. Despite finding no human bones or teeth in the layer, they obtained enough genetic information to determine the ancestry of the people who had occupied the site. "Sedimentary DNA allows us to recover genetic information from periods where human remains are missing," says senior author Ron Pinhasi, Department of Evolutionary Anthropology at the University of Vienna, whose team led this study. "This gives us a way to connect archaeological layers with the genetic ancestry of the people who occupied a site." The results indicate that western European ancestry persisted in the region through the Last Glacial Maximum, a period when enormous ice sheets reached their greatest extent during the last Ice Age. This supports the idea that the Iberian Peninsula, which includes present-day Spain and Portugal, served as an important refuge for prehistoric humans during some of the coldest conditions of the Ice Age. Another revealing discovery came from southern Italy, where researchers examined the genetic remains of Ostuni1b, a male fetus believed to be the son of a previously studied woman known as Ostuni1. Genetic analysis suggests that the child's father likely belonged to the same ancestral population as his mother. However, the parents were not closely related, offering evidence that mating patterns within these ancient communities may have helped limit inbreeding. This finding adds another dimension to the emerging picture of prehistoric European societies. Even as some populations maintained relatively stable genetic ancestry within their home regions, they could also participate in broader networks of genetic exchange spanning considerable distances. Together, the discoveries show that long-term regional continuity and widespread genetic connections were not mutually exclusive. Both helped shape the population history of Ice Age Europe. Building on these results, Gelabert and his colleagues are now combining DNA recovered from ancient sediments with advanced proteomic techniques, which examine proteins for clues about past life. Their goal is to investigate the earliest expansions of modern humans across Europe, including how these populations interacted with carnivores in places where bones and other organic remains are scarce. top.title: Scientists discover that some “unhealthy” diets can boost cancer immunotherapy in mice
top.summary: In a surprising discovery, scientists found that certain diets associated with obesity can make cancer immunotherapy more effective in mice, challenging traditional assumptions about diet and cancer treatment. The findings suggest that the secret may lie in how food interacts with gut bacteria to strengthen the immune system's response to cancer.
top.text: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected connection between diet and cancer treatment. In a surprising finding, certain diets typically considered "unhealthy" or "fattening" actually improved responses to a common form of cancer immunotherapy in mice. The discovery suggests that the success of cancer treatment may depend not only on which bacteria live in the gut, but also on the foods that help those bacteria thrive. "There is a synergistic relationship between the bacteria that reside in our GI tract, and the food we eat," said Daniela Quail, Associate Professor in the Department of Physiology and Principal Investigator at the Rosalind & Morris Goodman Cancer Institute. "Even with the right composition of bacteria in your gut, the foods you eat to nourish those populations can determine whether or not you respond to treatment," said Quail. Quail co-led the research, which examined how diet influences the effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors. These widely used immunotherapy drugs help the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. Other senior researchers involved in the study included McGill scientist Logan Walsh and CR-CHUM collaborators Bertrand Routy and Arielle Elkrief. The findings were published in Nature . One of the most unexpected discoveries was that some diets associated with weight gain appeared to make immunotherapy more effective, challenging assumptions about the relationship between nutrition and cancer treatment. "Our findings were surprising because they highlighted a benefit of some obesogenic diets," she said. "That tells us the relationship between diet and cancer treatment is more complex than a simple message to eat healthy and exercise." However, the researchers emphasize that these results should not encourage cancer patients to consume diets that promote obesity. Excess weight carries established health risks, and the findings do not demonstrate that adopting such diets would improve cancer treatment in humans. Instead, the scientists want to understand how different foods influence the gut microbiome, the enormous community of trillions of bacteria that inhabit the digestive system. Identifying the mechanisms responsible for the improved treatment responses could eventually help researchers develop safer ways to make cancer immunotherapy more effective. The investigation grew out of a longstanding puzzle in cancer research known as the "obesity paradox." Obesity is generally linked to a greater risk of developing cancer and dying from the disease. Yet several studies have found that cancer patients with a higher body mass index (BMI) sometimes respond more favorably to immune checkpoint inhibitors. To investigate this apparent contradiction, the research team tested 12 different diets in mice. Surprisingly, some diets associated with obesity improved the animals' responses to immunotherapy, even when they were consumed for relatively short periods. These results suggest that the apparent treatment advantage associated with obesity may not be primarily caused by excess body weight. Instead, the explanation could involve the combined influence of diet and gut bacteria on the immune system. By uncovering how these interactions affect cancer treatment, researchers hope to identify new approaches that reproduce the beneficial effects without exposing patients to the health risks associated with obesity. The study, "Diet-microbiome synergy underlies obesity-associated immunotherapy efficacy," was published in Nature by McGill PhD graduate Lysanne Desharnais, Daniela Quail, and their collaborators. top.title: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
top.summary: A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.
top.text: For decades, explanations for why some children struggle with reading have often focused on two factors: intelligence and the ability to process visual information. Children who read easily have frequently been assumed to be more intelligent, while those who struggle have sometimes been viewed as less capable. Another common belief is that reading difficulties arise primarily from problems interpreting the words and letters on a page. However, a major new study challenges these assumptions, suggesting that the abilities most important for reading success may be very different from what many people expect. Dr. Daniel Hajovsky, an associate professor in Texas A&M University's Department of Educational Psychology, led one of the most extensive investigations to date into how cognitive abilities relate to reading performance. The research brought together scientists from the University of Kansas, St. John's University, Montclair State University and Temple University to examine which mental skills best predict reading development and why some children encounter difficulties. To investigate these relationships, the researchers combined 50,000 correlations drawn from 137 cognitive and achievement test batteries into a single statistical model. This large-scale approach allowed them to assess the contribution of individual mental abilities to reading performance while also helping clarify why previous studies had sometimes produced conflicting conclusions. The findings revealed several surprises. Visual processing showed no meaningful relationship with reading ability across the analysis. General intelligence was associated with reading performance, but its influence was considerably smaller than some earlier research had suggested. Instead, two less frequently discussed abilities emerged as particularly important predictors of reading success: auditory processing and comprehension-knowledge. "One notable finding was that general intelligence was less dominant than in some earlier meta-analyses," Hajovsky said. "Broad abilities such as comprehension-knowledge and auditory processing played strong, specific roles in reading beyond general intelligence, especially for decoding and comprehension." Auditory processing involves recognizing and distinguishing the individual sounds that make up spoken words. For example, a child needs to identify the separate sounds within a word to understand how those sounds correspond to written letters. This skill helps support decoding, the process of working out how written words are pronounced. Comprehension-knowledge refers to the vocabulary, concepts and background information a child has accumulated through learning and everyday experiences. Having this foundation makes it easier to understand the meaning of words, sentences and longer passages. Together, these two abilities were more reliable predictors of reading performance than any other skills examined in the study. Other cognitive functions, including memory, reasoning and mental processing speed, also contributed to reading development, although they played more supporting roles. The results suggest that reading is not simply a reflection of overall intelligence or how effectively a child processes visual information. Instead, it depends on several interconnected abilities, with language-related skills playing especially important roles. The research could help educators better understand why individual students experience reading difficulties. Rather than treating all reading problems as the same, teachers may be able to identify particular weaknesses and provide instruction that addresses those needs. For families, the findings also offer an encouraging message. A child who has trouble reading is not necessarily less intelligent or incapable of becoming a strong reader. Difficulties may instead reflect specific abilities that need additional development and support. "Strengthening foundational skills at home, even the ones that seem simple, can have meaningful effects on more advanced reading abilities," Hajovsky said. "Struggles in reading are not a sign of low ability but often reflect one specific skill that needs strengthening within a larger system that works together." The findings highlight the value of helping children build essential reading skills through consistent support, both in the classroom and at home. According to Hajovsky, the most effective approach involves cooperation among schools, parents, and communities. Reading develops through a network of connected skills, and strengthening those foundations one step at a time can help children become more confident and capable readers. top.title: A 50-year-old mystery of vanishing frogs reveals a hidden killer
top.summary: A nearly 50-year-old mystery involving disappearing frogs in Brazil may finally be solved, with scientists uncovering evidence that a deadly fungus swept through the region and devastated vulnerable species. Remarkably, many frog populations have since rebounded, suggesting they developed greater tolerance to the disease that once threatened their survival.
top.text: For nearly 50 years, scientists have struggled to explain why frogs began disappearing from Brazil's Atlantic Forest, one of the world's richest regions for amphibian diversity. Beginning in the 1970s, researchers documented dramatic population declines, but the cause of these losses remained uncertain. Now, scientists have uncovered compelling evidence pointing to a deadly fungal disease as the likely explanation. The findings, published in Molecular Ecology , come from researchers at the Center for Conservation Genomics at the Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute (NZCBI) and Pennsylvania State University (PSU). The suspected culprit is chytridiomycosis, often called chytrid, a disease caused by the microscopic fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis . Scientists believe the pathogen originated in Asia before spreading around the world during the 1970s and 1980s. However, the fungus was not formally identified and described until 1999, long after devastating amphibian declines had begun. By then, hundreds of amphibian species worldwide had been driven toward extinction, and some had already disappeared. Because so many populations collapsed before scientists knew the fungus existed, determining whether it was responsible has been particularly difficult. "After almost 50 years, we still aren't confident what caused many historical amphibian die-offs, making these declines some of the most enduring cold cases in wildlife epidemiology," said Jack Boyette, an NZCBI graduate fellow and doctoral candidate at PSU who led the research. One of these longstanding mysteries centers on the Boracéia Biological Station in Brazil's Atlantic Forest, where amphibian populations experienced severe declines between 1979 and 1982. Some researchers previously suggested that climate change or unusually extreme weather might have triggered the disappearances. The new findings, however, provide evidence that an emerging fungal disease was spreading through the area at precisely the same time. "While environmental factors could have played a role, our findings most directly implicate the chytrid fungus, revealing that regional invasion of the pathogen coincided with these unexplained amphibian disappearances," Boyette said. To investigate what happened, the researchers turned to an unexpected source of evidence: frogs preserved in museum collections decades earlier. The Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History houses specimens collected by William Ronald Heyer, a former curator of amphibians and reptiles. Heyer conducted five collecting expeditions at Boracéia, including two during the 1970s before the major population declines and three during the 1980s after the die-offs had occurred. These preserved animals offered scientists a rare opportunity to examine the period before and after the mysterious disappearances. By testing specimens collected at different times, researchers could investigate when the pathogen arrived and how rapidly it spread. The team analyzed samples from more than 370 preserved amphibians representing 17 species, searching for evidence of chytrid infection and tracking how frequently the fungus appeared over time. The results revealed a striking change. None of the specimens collected before 1979 showed evidence of chytrid infection. Among those collected during the 1980s, however, more than half tested positive for the fungus. This sharp increase suggests that the pathogen arrived and spread through the local amphibian community around the same time that frog populations were collapsing. Species that suffered the most severe declines showed no detectable signs of infection in the preserved specimens. Meanwhile, species whose populations remained relatively stable frequently carried the fungus. At first glance, these findings might seem to contradict the idea that chytrid caused the disappearances. The researchers believe the explanation may lie in differences in how individual species respond to the disease. Some frogs may have been naturally capable of tolerating the infection, allowing them to survive even when the fungus was present. More vulnerable species, on the other hand, may have died so quickly after becoming infected that few or no infected individuals were ever collected. "It's important to keep in mind that not all species suffered catastrophic losses at Boracéia," Boyette said. "The species that didn't decline may have naturally tolerated the fungus, allowing them to become infected without suffering mass mortality. By contrast, the species that declined most dramatically may have been so susceptible that infected frogs died before Heyer could collect them." Together, the results suggest that chytrid spread rapidly among frogs with little previous exposure to the disease, with potentially devastating consequences for species unable to withstand infection. For Michael Campana, a genomicist at NZCBI who contributed to the research, the findings demonstrate the extraordinary scientific value of natural history museums. Specimens preserved many decades ago can contain biological evidence that researchers at the time had no way of recognizing. Modern testing methods now make it possible to revisit these collections and investigate outbreaks that occurred long before the responsible pathogens were discovered. "Museum collectors could not have anticipated how important their collections would be to our modern conservation challenges, but without them, we would never be able to detect pathogens that went unnoticed for decades and reconstruct disease outbreaks that would otherwise remain a mystery," Campana said. Understanding these past outbreaks could also help scientists anticipate future threats. One growing concern involves another fungal pathogen, B. salamandrivorans , which is threatening salamander populations in Europe and could pose a serious danger to salamanders in North America. By reconstructing how earlier fungal diseases emerged, spread, and affected different species, researchers hope to improve their ability to recognize and respond to similar threats before they cause widespread damage. Despite the devastating losses recorded decades ago, the latest findings also offer encouraging evidence of recovery. Working with researchers from the University of São Paulo, the team made six visits to Boracéia between 2022 and 2024 to investigate the amphibians living there today. Of the 17 species represented in Heyer's historical museum collection, researchers located 12 during their modern surveys. The remaining five were not found, leaving their current status uncertain and raising concerns that some may have disappeared from the site entirely. Nevertheless, the surveys indicate that most amphibian species at Boracéia have recovered since the severe declines of the early 1980s. The fungus has not disappeared. Chytrid infections are still present among local frogs, but the pattern of infection suggests that species once heavily affected by the disease may have developed greater tolerance over successive generations. That increased tolerance could help explain why many populations have survived and rebounded despite continuing exposure to the pathogen. The findings highlight an important distinction between infection and mortality. A species can carry a dangerous pathogen without necessarily suffering catastrophic losses, particularly if its members can tolerate the infection. Although the evidence strongly implicates chytrid in the historic declines at Boracéia, the researchers caution that their findings apply to this particular location. The results cannot automatically explain amphibian disappearances elsewhere in the Atlantic Forest. Still, the study provides a compelling explanation for a longstanding local mystery and demonstrates how scientists can use historical specimens to reconstruct outbreaks that would otherwise remain poorly understood. Scientists believe the pathogen originated in Asia before spreading around the world during the 1970s and 1980s.

One of these longstanding mysteries centers on the Boracéia Biological Station in Brazil's Atlantic Forest, where amphibian populations experienced severe declines between 1979 and 1982.
Heyer conducted five collecting expeditions at Boracéia, including two during the 1970s before the major population declines and three during the 1980s after the die-offs had occurred.
By testing specimens collected at different times, researchers could investigate when the pathogen arrived and how rapidly it spread.
The team analyzed samples from more than 370 preserved amphibians representing 17 species, searching for evidence of chytrid infection and tracking how frequently the fungus appeared over time.
None of the specimens collected before 1979 showed evidence of chytrid infection.

top.title: Nearly 1 in 5 people in the US think about food even when they are not hungry
top.summary: "Food noise" refers to intrusive thoughts about and cravings for food, whether or not a person is hungry. The phenomenon has become widely discussed on social media, in traditional media and in commercials for GLP-1 receptor agonist weight-loss medications. Because the term has only emerged in recent years, not much is known about who experiences food noise, and there is not even a universally accepted scientific definition.

top.title: Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response
top.summary: A new study suggests that ultra-processed foods may influence children's developing brains in ways that encourage weight gain. Researchers from USC studied 46 children ages 7 to 10 and found that those who ate more ultra-processed foods showed stronger activity in the brain's reward system when viewing tempting foods like cookies and French fries. These heightened brain responses were linked to greater increases in body fat and body mass index (BMI) one year later, suggesting that the brain's sensitivity to food cues may help explain why ultra-processed diets are associated with obesity.
top.text: Children who consume more ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may have stronger brain responses to tempting foods, potentially helping explain why these products are associated with weight gain. A new study published in JAMA Network Open found that children who ate more of these foods showed heightened activity in the brain's reward system when looking at pictures of appetizing foods. Those stronger responses were also associated with increases in body fat over the following year. Ultra-processed foods include many everyday products, such as breakfast cereals, packaged bread, and instant soups. They are manufactured to be appealing, convenient, and able to remain fresh for extended periods. Many contain artificial sweeteners, coloring agents, and other ingredients rarely used in home cooking. These products make up a substantial portion of children's diets, accounting for approximately 67% of the calories consumed by children in the United States. Previous research has associated ultra-processed food consumption with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. However, scientists are still trying to understand the biological processes that might explain these connections. The new investigation, supported in part by the National Institutes of Health, combined magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), dietary assessments, and measurements of children's body composition to explore whether the brain's response to food could play a role. "Children's brains are still developing, habits are still forming and food preferences are still being made. It's an important period where the brain is very sensitive to food and the food environment," said the study's senior author, Kathleen A. Page, MD, professor of medicine and pediatrics and co-chief of the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. "We're particularly interested in understanding these processes in children, because we believe that intervening early could make a real difference." To investigate these connections, the research team studied 46 children between the ages of seven and 10 who were enrolled in the ongoing BrainChild study, which examines factors contributing to diabetes and obesity. Every participant had a healthy weight when the research began, giving scientists an opportunity to investigate potential warning signs before excess weight developed. At the start of the study, the children underwent brain scans while looking at pictures of appealing foods (such as cookies or French fries). Researchers also gathered information about their diets and recorded several health measurements, including body mass index (BMI), body fat percentage, and waist circumference. After one year, the team measured these physical characteristics again to identify changes. The brain scans revealed a notable pattern. Children who consumed larger amounts of ultra-processed foods showed greater activity in the dorsal striatum when viewing food pictures. This part of the brain helps regulate reward and motivation, making it particularly relevant to how people respond to desirable foods. Importantly, children with stronger responses in this brain region also tended to experience greater increases in BMI and body fat percentage over the next year. The findings suggest that heightened sensitivity to food cues may be one factor connecting ultra-processed diets with subsequent weight gain. By the end of the study, children who consumed more ultra-processed foods generally had higher BMI, greater body fat percentage, and larger waist circumference. The researchers then examined whether differences in brain activity could help account for these associations. When they adjusted their analysis to consider the children's responses in the dorsal striatum, the relationship between ultra-processed food intake and BMI became 31% weaker. The corresponding association with body fat percentage decreased by 44%. These reductions suggest that the brain's reward response may help explain part of the relationship between ultra-processed food consumption and changes in body composition. Although the results do not demonstrate that these foods directly alter brain function, they provide a possible biological explanation for an association that has been observed in previous research. "This study goes beyond just understanding that UPFs affect weight gain," Page said. "It actually gives us insight into the neurobiological underpinnings by which these foods may be linked to body composition over time." The researchers caution that improving children's diets cannot depend entirely on individual families. Ultra-processed products are often inexpensive, widely available, and easy to prepare, making them practical choices for households facing financial or time constraints. "Changing the food environment to help people access healthier, more minimally processed foods is an important part of the solution," Page said. There are also important limitations to consider. Because the study was observational, it cannot determine whether eating ultra-processed foods directly causes heightened brain activity or increases in body weight. The findings establish relationships between these factors, but additional research is needed to determine whether one causes another. Page hopes to address that question in a future intervention study. The proposed research would provide children who regularly consume ultra-processed foods with more minimally processed alternatives. Scientists could then examine whether changing their diets affects how their brains respond to food images and whether any differences are associated with reduced weight gain. Meanwhile, the BrainChild study will continue tracking participants as they move through puberty and into early adulthood. By monitoring brain development, body composition, dietary patterns, and general health over time, researchers hope to gain a clearer picture of how childhood nutrition may influence long-term health.
