top.title: Consuming colorful produce may help reduce COPD-related inflammation, flare-ups
top.summary: Eating a diet rich in red, yellow and orange fruits and vegetables may help reduce inflammation and exacerbations associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), according to a new study in the September 2026 issue of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Diseases: Journal of the COPD Foundation.

top.title: Shockwave therapy may ease frozen shoulder pain, but lasting benefits remain uncertain
top.summary: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy probably reduces short-term pain linked to frozen shoulder, while manipulation under anesthesia—with or without steroid injections—probably improves short-term flexion (raising the arm forward and overhead) compared with usual care, finds a review of the latest trial evidence published by The BMJ.

top.title: Combining HIV prevention and addiction treatment in mobile clinics could save lives
top.summary: Results from a clinical trial in five major United States cities show that delivering integrated HIV and substance use disorder (SUD) services using peer navigation in mobile medical units reduced all-cause deaths by 71% compared with those among participants who received peer navigation to community-based services alone. While scientists found no difference in the use of daily, oral preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD) between the groups, the secondary outcome of reduced mortality was significant. The study is published in JAMA Psychiatry.

top.title: Rapid tau spread may explain why midlife Alzheimer's progresses more rapidly
top.summary: Patients with early-onset Alzheimer's disease, whose symptoms start before age 65, have more extensive deposits of tau, a hallmark protein of the condition, compared with patients whose symptoms start at 65-plus, a new study found. What's more, tau accumulates at more than twice the rate in younger compared to older patients and spreads widely throughout the brain.

top.title: Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss
top.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising link between Alzheimer’s-related protein buildup, disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, and fading memory. The findings suggest that hidden changes in how the brain processes memories overnight may contribute to age-related memory loss long before Alzheimer’s symptoms appear.
top.text: You walk out of the grocery store, ready to head home and make dinner. But as you scan the crowded parking lot, a frustrating question comes to mind. Where did you leave your car? You try to picture the spot, but the memory refuses to surface. Remembering personal experiences like these depends on episodic memory, which allows us to recall events from our lives. These memories help form the foundation of long-term memory, whether they involve a childhood milestone, such as the first day of elementary school, or something that happened just minutes earlier, like parking your car. This ability tends to weaken as we grow older. The sights, sounds, and other details associated with past experiences can become increasingly difficult to retrieve. Scientists still do not fully understand why this happens. Although some memory decline is a common part of aging, the changes can become far more severe in people developing Alzheimer's disease. A new study from researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, offers important clues about what may be happening inside the aging brain. Neuroscientist Omer Sharon and his colleagues, working under the direction of former Berkeley sleep researcher Matthew Walker, discovered a connection between disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, declining memory performance, and the accumulation of tau, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease. The findings suggest that tau buildup in the brain's frontal cortex is linked to changes in the coordinated electrical activity that helps preserve memories overnight. "This is the first time we've shown this relationship between tau and how it messes with memory consolidation by attenuating traveling slow waves that originate in the frontal cortex," said Sharon, a postdoctoral researcher at UC Berkeley's Center for Human Sleep Science. Sleep involves several distinct stages, each associated with different patterns of brain activity. Rapid eye movement sleep is particularly recognizable because the eyes move beneath closed eyelids and most dreaming takes place during this stage. However, another stage, known as non-REM sleep, is especially important for maintaining healthy brain function. During this deeper stage of sleep, when dreaming is limited or absent, large groups of neurons briefly become inactive and then active again in a coordinated sequence. These synchronized changes produce slow electrical waves that spread across the brain, typically beginning in the frontal cortex. "Each slow wave reflects an enormous population of neurons switching off and back on together," Sharon said. "Our study shows that for memory, it's critical that these events cascade in sequence across large parts of the brain. This coordinated shutdown has been observed only during deep sleep, and may be one reason why we sleep." The researchers found that this carefully organized activity becomes less coordinated as tau accumulates in the aging brain. Instead of traveling together across broad regions, the waves become more scattered and cover shorter distances. These changes are associated with weaker memory consolidation, declining cognitive abilities, and Alzheimer's disease. To investigate the relationship, the scientists monitored sleeping brain activity using electroencephalograms (EEGs). They compared cognitively healthy young adults in their early 20s with older participants ranging from their mid-60s to mid-70s. The differences were striking. In younger participants, groups of slow waves moved together across distances roughly equivalent to the width of a hand on the scalp. Among older adults, the waves typically traveled less far and appeared more independently, rather than moving in coordinated groups. The team also examined whether these changes were associated with tau accumulation. Working with Dr. William Jagust, a UC Berkeley professor emeritus of public health and neuroscience, the researchers used positron emission tomography (PET) scans to examine the brains of older participants. This imaging technique uses radioactive tracers introduced into the bloodstream to reveal biological activity and the distribution of specific substances. The scans showed that greater tau buildup in the frontal cortex was associated with a breakdown in the longer traveling waves normally seen during deep sleep. Importantly, these changes were present in people who had not developed Alzheimer's disease. "These people did not have Alzheimer's," Sharon said. "They had tau in their brains, but with subclinical impacts. Their memory decline was within the normal range for their age." Sharon explained that early Alzheimer's related changes can vary considerably in severity. The amount of tau present in the brain is associated with cognitive performance, even when a person's memory abilities remain within the expected range for their age. The researchers wanted to determine whether the altered sleep patterns were associated with actual differences in how well people remembered information. To test this, participants learned pairs of associated words in the evening. The following day, they were asked to recall what they had learned, allowing the scientists to evaluate how effectively the memories had been retained overnight. Participants whose slow brain waves traveled shorter distances and appeared more isolated generally remembered fewer word associations. The researchers called these disconnected patterns "lonely waves." The team also tracked a subset of participants over several years to see how their brains changed with time. Among those whose frontal cortex tau levels increased, the slow waves became less coordinated, and their ability to retain newly learned information overnight declined. These observations provide evidence of a relationship between tau accumulation, changes in deep sleep brain activity, and worsening episodic memory. However, they do not establish that tau buildup directly causes memory loss or that disrupted waves are the mechanism responsible. Because PET scans are costly and require specialized facilities, the scientists sought another way to investigate the relationship between Alzheimer's related proteins and sleep activity. They collaborated with neurologist Yo-El Ju at Washington University in St. Louis to analyze spinal fluid from a separate group of older adults. The goal was to determine whether measurements of Alzheimer's associated proteins would reveal patterns similar to those seen with brain imaging. Unlike PET scans, the spinal fluid measurements could not identify tau accumulation specifically within the frontal cortex. Nevertheless, the results pointed in the same direction. People whose sleeping brains produced more isolated slow waves had higher ratios of tau to amyloid, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease, in their spinal fluid. The consistency between these independent groups and testing methods strengthened the researchers' confidence in the findings. "It's collected in a totally different place and in a different cohort, so I think that adds to the strength of the evidence," Sharon said. Together, the sleep recordings, brain scans, spinal fluid analyses, and memory assessments suggest that tau accumulation is associated with a particular disruption of brain activity during deep sleep. "This longitudinal correlation suggests that Alzheimer's disease pathology is associated with a disruption of this main sleep feature," Sharon said. Although memory often declines with age, the new research indicates that the process may involve more than simply growing older. Changes associated with Alzheimer's disease, particularly tau accumulation in regions responsible for generating widespread slow waves, may help explain why some people experience greater difficulty retaining memories. top.title: Why do blind people and musicians hear pitch better? New research suggests they have less internal noise
top.summary: People who have lived most of their lives blind often have extraordinary hearing abilities. In new research published in the Journal of Neuroscience, my colleagues and I discovered that this ability arises from how their auditory systems are able to more consistently and reliably process sounds compared with people who aren't blind. And interestingly, sighted musicians seem to enhance their hearing through a similar mechanism.

top.title: Mammograms can do more than detect breast cancer—they also offer important clues on heart health
top.summary: If you're a woman over 40, you have no doubt heard your doctor tell you to get a mammogram as part of routine screening for breast cancer. But there's another reason, too.

top.title: Maternal vitamin A deficiency may increase risk of larger babies
top.summary: A study in Norway has identified a link between a mother's vitamin A levels and her baby's birth weight. The study shows that over 43% of the women had low vitamin A levels during the latter part of their pregnancy. While almost no one had levels classified as a severe vitamin A deficiency, two out of five had insufficient levels. The study examined 723 women who experienced entirely normal pregnancies.

top.title: Virtual reality tied to lower presurgery anxiety in kids
top.summary: Children who used a virtual reality (VR) headset before surgery showed reduced self-reported distress and fear, along with lower heart rate and blood pressure, according to a new study published Nov. 5 in the journal PLOS Digital Health by Dayanjan Wijesinghe of Virginia Commonwealth University, U.S., and colleagues.

top.title: Updated guidance refines how doctors assess cardiogenic shock and track treatment response
top.summary: The Society for Cardiovascular Angiography & Interventions (SCAI) has released the 2026 SCAI SHOCK Classification Expert Consensus Update, providing refined guidance to help clinicians from diverse settings prioritize and recognize inadequate organ perfusion across a broad range of shock presentations, assess shock severity over time, and determine whether treatment is restoring adequate circulation.

top.title: Two compounds target drug-resistant brain cancer cells in laboratory tests
top.summary: Cancer remains among the most deadly diseases worldwide. Globally, more than 300,000 new cases of brain cancer are reported each year, with glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer, accounting for over 250,000 deaths. The current standard of care involves the use of temozolomide (TMZ), a chemotherapy medication. However, the tumor can be difficult to control because cancer cells evolve to evade the effects of such treatments. Thus, finding new ways to target these cells is an important area in cancer research.

top.title: New species of ground-dwelling bird, the largest of its kind, identified in same cave as Homo floresiensis
top.summary: In 2009, researchers working in the Liang Bua cave on Flores Island came across a leg bone. The 190,000–120,000-year-old fossil was identified as a bird bone and set aside. Like many bird bones before it, it was overlooked and left to collect dust.

top.title: Reversing radiation-activated immune suppression in cancer
top.summary: Researchers at the University of Chicago have identified a mechanism to make immune cells reprogrammed by radiation therapy attack tumors rather than protect them. The study, published in Cancer Cell, shows that radiation activates a protein called TET2 on immune cells in bone marrow, where it removes chemical tags from RNA and locks these cells into an immune-suppressing state.

top.title: Predicting jumping genes' roles in changing genome size
top.summary: A genome contains all of the DNA of every living organism, but its contents don't stop there—most of these structures also contain snippets of DNA that can copy and paste themselves to "infect" a genome, expanding its size. Precisely why that happens remains a mystery.

top.title: Zombies are real—just ask the parasites taking over the bodies and brains of insects and rodents
top.summary: Zombies have taken many forms in popular culture. In Michael Jackson's "Thriller" music video, corpses climb out of their graves and perform an impressively coordinated dance. In HBO's "The Last of Us," a fungus infects humans, takes over their bodies and turns them into hosts that help spread the infection. Even Plankton has tried his hand at taking control of another organism in "SpongeBob SquarePants."

top.title: Are Counter-Strike players better at decision-making? Study reveals faster brain processing in expert gamers
top.summary: Expert Counter-Strike players could make ideal candidates for fast-paced emergency service response jobs requiring split-second decision-making, according to a new University of Sheffield study aiming to debunk myths about video games.

top.title: Plants' immune memory hints at new crop breeding approach
top.summary: A study published in Nature Communications, led by professor Jurriaan Ton and Dr. Adam Hannan Parker at the University of Sheffield, has identified mechanisms by which plants maintain and reset stress memory from past infections. This immune memory enables plants to defend themselves more effectively against harmful bacteria and mildews, which are increasingly threatening our crop and food production.

top.title: Tiny fossils show brittle stars gathered around a dead whale 9.5 million years ago
top.summary: Tiny skeletal plates recovered beside fossil whale bones in southern Denmark offer a rare glimpse of life around a whale carcass approximately 9.5 million years ago. Researchers have identified a new species of brittle star, Ophiura huebnerjenseni, from the Gram Clay Pit and suggest it represents the first fossil record of brittle stars associated with a whale fall.

top.title: Pulsars set first mass limits on supermassive black hole pairs in the early universe
top.summary: So far, observations by instruments including the James Webb Space Telescope have revealed the presence of surprisingly massive black holes in the early universe. Even less than a billion years after the Big Bang, some of these bodies already weighed billions of times the mass of the sun, and to date, astronomers are unclear as to how they could have grown so large so quickly.

top.title: Trust in influencers grows more important in predicting buying intentions over time, analysis finds
top.summary: A meta-analysis of empirical studies involving more than 31,000 participants has revealed the factors that affect the level of influence of so-called social media influencers. Those factors include credibility, expertise, attractiveness and perceived similarity to their followers. They are, the work shows, positively associated with the attitude of consumers toward the brands mentioned or promoted by those influencers and, in turn, their purchasing intentions. Details of the analysis are published in the International Journal of Internet Marketing and Advertising.

top.title: A sweeter future? AI helps scientists discover new sugar substitutes
top.summary: Researchers Dr. Shayma El-Atawneh and professor Amiram Goldblum at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem have developed a new computational framework that identified 92 promising candidates for future sugar substitutes from more than 50 million chemical compounds. The study, published in the journal Food Chemistry, demonstrates how artificial intelligence and molecular modeling could accelerate the discovery of new sweeteners while helping overcome one of the industry's persistent challenges: unwanted bitter aftertastes.

top.title: How do octopuses remember? Scientists uncover a surprising secret
top.summary: How does an octopus remember what it has learned? A new study led by Dr. Ana Luiza Turchetti-Maia, Dr. Tal Shomrat and professor Binyamin (Benny) Hochner—researchers from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and Ruppin Academic Center—has uncovered a previously unknown molecular mechanism that may help explain how these remarkably intelligent animals form and maintain memories.

top.title: Heavy hydrogen in 3I/ATLAS's methane points to a frigid birthplace
top.summary: The interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS carries a chemical clue to conditions in the planetary system of its origin, locked away long before it reached our sun. Its methane signature is unusually rich in heavy hydrogen, suggesting that the comet's frozen ingredients took shape in an intensely cold environment around another star—or in the cloud that preceded it.

top.title: Collective human metabolism produces 2 billion metric tons of CO₂ a year, global study estimates
top.summary: A University of Bath–led study has estimated that the carbon dioxide produced by humans as our bodies turn food into energy rose by 74% between 1985 and 2015, reaching 2.05 billion metric tons a year. Researchers say the findings could help scientists better understand where carbon comes from, where it goes and how human activity fits into the bigger picture.

top.title: Extra weight may be aging your brain faster than you think
top.summary: A major 24-year study involving more than 8,200 adults suggests that excess body weight may accelerate brain aging, leading to faster declines in memory, concentration, and decision-making skills. The connection was particularly strong among people over 65, raising concerns about the long-term effects of obesity on brain health.
top.text: Carrying excess weight may affect more than physical health. New research from the University of Georgia suggests that having a higher body mass index may also speed up cognitive decline, potentially causing memory and thinking abilities to deteriorate more quickly with age. Some cognitive changes are a natural part of getting older. Remembering information, thinking clearly, and processing new details can become more difficult over time. For healthy adults, however, these changes are usually relatively mild and develop gradually. The new findings suggest that excess body weight may accelerate this process. Researchers found that people with higher body mass index (BMI) experienced faster declines in memory, overall cognitive performance, and executive functioning. These abilities are essential for everyday activities such as concentrating, planning, organizing tasks, and regulating emotions. To investigate the connection, the research team analyzed data from a nationally representative study that tracked more than 8,200 adults over age 50 for 24 years. The results revealed a consistent relationship between body weight and cognitive health. Each one-point increase in BMI was associated with a faster rate of cognitive decline, suggesting that even relatively small differences in body weight could matter over time. The association was strongest at the eighth year of the study, and adults older than 65 showed the most pronounced effects. Despite the concerning findings, researchers also identified a potentially encouraging opportunity to protect brain health. Managing body weight may help slow cognitive decline, with possible benefits becoming apparent within just two years. "We found that if people managed their weight, they could significantly lower their rate of cognitive decline in just two years," said Suhang Song, the study's lead author and an assistant professor at the University of Georgia's College of Public Health. "That makes BMI one of the most easily modifiable risk factors when it comes to aging well." Obesity, generally defined as a BMI of 30 or higher, has been associated with poorer brain health. However, scientists are still working to understand exactly why carrying excess body weight may interfere with memory and other cognitive abilities. Several biological processes could help explain the connection. Excess weight may promote inflammation, impair blood circulation, and contribute to insulin resistance. Together, these changes could increase the likelihood of cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease, and other forms of dementia. The findings are particularly relevant given how widespread obesity has become in the United States. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, approximately two in five Americans meet the criteria for obesity when BMI is used as the sole measure. Some scientists argue that BMI alone does not provide a complete picture of obesity. They support a broader definition that also considers waist measurements and medical conditions associated with excess weight. Using those additional criteria, the estimated proportion of Americans classified as having obesity rises to 75%. The potential connection between obesity and cognitive decline is especially concerning as dementia becomes increasingly common. More than 7 million Americans currently live with dementia, and researchers expect that number to double by 2050. Although the study does not establish that excess weight directly causes cognitive decline, its findings highlight body weight as a potentially important factor in maintaining cognitive health. Because weight can be managed, researchers believe it could offer an opportunity to reduce the risk of worsening memory and thinking abilities as people grow older. "There are no cures for dementia," Song said, "which is why it is critical to identify and address any modifiable risk factors we can find to prevent it." The research was published in the Journal of Neurology . top.title: A Feejee Mermaid on display in Colorado may shock and intrigue – but it’s no longer considered a ‘missing link’ on the evolutionary tree

top.text: Mermaids have inhabited world folklore and mythology for centuries. Ancient Babylonians worshipped Oannes , a human-fish hybrid; sirens populated Greek mythology ; and fairy tales such as “ The Little Mermaid ” have made this figure a pop culture icon. During the 1800s, American showman P.T. Barnum brought the Feejee Mermaid to the American public. Presented at the American Museum, run by Barnum in Manhattan from 1841 to 1865 , as “ The Greatest Curiosity in the World ” and said to have originated in the “Feejee Islands,” the creature inspired debates about science and evolution. Some people believed it was a missing link in the evolutionary chain between aquatic and terrestrial life. I recently viewed a Feejee Mermaid replica on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science as part of the “ Mythic Creatures: Dragons, Unicorns and Mermaids” temporary exhibit . As a folklorist , I’m intrigued by how this mermaid subverted Americans’ expectations that mermaids are alluring and how it sparked an interplay between science and myth. A Feejee Mermaid is a type of traditional art form that originated in Japan and the East Indies more than 400 years ago. It came to Americans in 1842, when Barnum claimed to display a “specimen” at the American Museum in New York City. In the Japanese version, the lower half was a fish attached to an upper half of a monkey or made of papier-mâché. Barnum’s was a mixture of a monkey and a fish, but the replica on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science has a papier-mâché upper half. Feejee Mermaids were often preserved by being coated in clay . Mammalian-fish hybrid creatures have a role in Japanese folklore through the ningyo , which are a mermaidlike yokai, a supernatural being thought to have the power to either curse or grant eternal life. Unlike Western mermaids, ningyo were grotesque. The Feejee Mermaid that became part of Barnum’s exhibition was created by a Japanese fisherman in the early 19th century. He claimed to have caught the specimen and said it prophesied a sterility epidemic. The only cure for the townsfolk, the fisherman said, came through owning a picture of the mermaid. Samuel Barrett Eades, an American sailor, purchased the Feejee Mermaid and willed it to his son, who then sold it to Moses Kimball , a curator at the Boston Museum, in 1842. In his autobiography, Barnum details the scheme he devised after Kimball showed him the Feejee Mermaid. Barnum sent letters to newspapers, describing how a “Dr. Griffin,” who was really his hoaxing accomplice Levi Lyman, was in possession of the mermaid skeleton. He further spread the word by distributing thousands of pamphlets throughout New York City that detailed when the mermaid would be on display and highlighted the seductive nature of mermaids. However, when the public arrived at the American Museum, much to their surprise, they found Barnum’s grotesque version. Barnum himself described it as “an ugly dried-up, black-looking diminutive specimen, about three feet long. Its mouth was open, its tail turned over and its arms thrown up, giving it the appearance of having died in great agony.” The Feejee Mermaid on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science, and owned by the Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology, may or may not be the one shown by Barnum. The museum says it is a replica. The original was likely destroyed or disfigured in a fire at Barnum’s museum or the Boston Museum. The object on display looks quite different compared to original descriptions of the Feejee Mermaid. As originally shown, it was said to be much more monkeylike, and artistic renderings of it from the period matched Barnum’s descriptions. Feejee Mermaids, as displayed in America, are characteristic of a “ sideshow gaff ” that interested Victorian audiences due to debates about evolution and science. In fact, 18th-century Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus had left space for mermaids in the evolutionary tree . The Feejee Mermaid, as it blended human and animal characteristics, folklore and science, spectacle and empiricism, displays how a monstrous hoax inspired fierce intellectual debates in 19th-century America.

top.title: ‘Epic’ blue wave helps Democrats take Congress in overwhelming rebuke to President Trump
top.summary: Election Day turned into a massive rebuke of President Donald Trump: a blue wave not seen in 20 years that was built on transforming the economy and rising prices into a central line of attack.
top.text: Voters turned out in massive numbers on Election Day to hand Democrats control of Congress, in a sweeping snub of President Donald Trump and Republicans. Democrats won several statewide races in places long considered GOP bastions , including races that were considered insurmountable even weeks ago . Democrats took control of the House and Senate , flipping Senate seats in Texas , South Carolina, North Carolina, Kansas and Ohio. The results reflected broad dissatisfaction across the country with Trump, his agenda and the candidates he had endorsed. The Conversation’s senior politics editor, Alfonso Serrano, spoke on election night with Charlie Hunt, a scholar at Boise State University who studies Congress and elections . It was obviously a strong showing for Democrats on Election Day, something that was even evident in the margin of some Democratic losses. What does it tell you, for example, that democratic socialist Angie Nixon fought a competitive race for the Senate in Florida? There is this big uniform shift toward the Democrats that we’re seeing really across virtually all kinds of locations and geographies and counties. What I think is particularly notable here, and something we were on the lookout for in this election, and we’re seeing it, is the substantial shift in the Hispanic vote from 2024 in places like Texas and Florida, where you’re getting these 30-to-35 point shifts from how Donald Trump performed in 2024. That was a big part of what helped him win , and it seems like it has snapped right back and even farther in the other direction. This is what made Florida, I think, closer than a lot of folks thought. It’s what put a number of really, really right-leaning districts in play, particularly in South Florida. And it looks like it is going to help Democrats keep the number of seats they had in Florida in the House that they had before the election, which is incredible when you consider that Florida did this mid-decade gerrymander to try to get them out of a bunch of those seats. Some rural areas of the country were also more competitive than expected, like North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, where Democrat Jaime Ager flipped a conservative district . What does that tell you? It’s definitely an indicator of at least one of these two things. One is just really massive Democratic turnout across the board. Regardless of where they live, Democrats were so enthusiastic and energized to turn out that they did so across all different types of districts and counties. It could also be an indicator of some cross-party voting, where Republicans are crossing over in some cases and voting for the Democrat. I don’t imagine there’s a ton of that, but in a lot of these close districts, and if you’ve got enough of those folks in places like Texas, it really does make a big difference, those small shifts. I think we’re probably also likely to see, and we saw some of this in the exit polling, a major shift in independent voters, unaffiliated voters, toward the Democrats, whereas in 2024 they had been closer to Trump. I’d like to go back to turnout briefly. Turnout looks like it was strong across the country. In Georgia, for example, Election Day’s turnout was on pace to beat turnout in the 2024 presidential elections. That’s unprecedented, at least in modern elections. In Texas, for example, in some counties we saw James Talarico getting as many raw votes as Kamala Harris did in a presidential election. This isn’t a very political science term, but that’s insane. In a midterm election you typically see 10% or 15% less turnout than you would in a presidential election. But Democrats voted in presidential-level numbers in a lot of these really key areas, and that’s explaining how they’re able to overperform at levels we haven’t seen in at least 20 years. Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars supporting Republican candidates, including some US$200 million in Texas to elect Ken Paxton for the Senate, who lost. What does that tell you about the influence of political spending? Republican PACs, super PACs and billionaire donors like Elon Musk may have raised more money compared to Democrats, but Democratic candidates themselves outraised Republican candidates through donors that gave directly to their campaigns. This is important for a couple of reasons. Number one, because candidates get much better rates on TV ad buys than outside spenders. And so they get more bang for their buck when they’re spending on advertisements, which is the most expensive component of any campaign. And more to the point, that is an indicator of sort of dedicated grassroots donors who turn into voters, whereas Musk gets one vote at the end of the day. And there is no amount of money that can make up for a really flawed candidate like Ken Paxton . And more to the point, a lot of this money, once you get into the tens, the hundreds of millions of dollars, a lot of the research talks about the diminishing returns that you get on that. Going from zero dollars spent to $10 million spent, that’s a very different kind of campaign. But once you go from $500 million to $510 million, that’s not going to get you a whole lot more votes. The territory that Democrats covered is unbelievable. The South Carolina Senate race went to Annie Andrews , the Democrat, which was unfathomable even a few months ago. Mississippi still appears to be somewhat in play. The blue wave turned into something approaching a tsunami. I think a lot of Democrats saw the polling and didn’t want to believe it or couldn’t bring themselves to believe it. But some of this late polling seems to have gotten things on the mark. What we’ve seen in these midterm elections is a massive rebuke of the last two years of the Trump administration, and a sort of blue wave of epic proportions toward the Democrats, the likes of which we haven’t seen in 20 or more years. It’s a huge confirmation of the approach that Democrats took in this election.

top.title: Flesh-eating screwworm is spreading in the US, threatening livestock and wildlife – hunters can be the first line of defense
top.summary: Over 100 screwworm cases have appeared in US animals in 2026, including in elk. How America’s 11.5 million hunters can help find these parasites and contain the spread.
top.text: For the first time in over 50 years, an infestation of the flesh-eating fly known as the New World screwworm ( Cochliomyia hominivorax ) is spreading on the U.S. mainland, and it is putting livestock and other animals at risk. The New World screwworm doesn’t just attack cattle. All warm-blooded animals are susceptible, including deer and elk, as well as small game, waterfowl and pets. That means hunters headed to the field this fall may be the most important line of defense for spotting this destructive parasite and keeping it from spreading further. As co-directors of the Mississippi State University deer lab , we believe the country’s millions of hunters can serve as a powerful early warning system by keeping a close eye on the state of wildlife they see. Wildlife agencies are already asking them to be vigilant and report any signs of screwworm infestations . Unlike other blowflies , New World screwworm larvae feed on living tissue rather than dead tissue. They lay eggs in open wounds or mucosal openings, such as the eyes and nose of livestock, deer or elk. Wounds as small as tick bites or scratches, as well as natural openings such as the umbilical stump on newborns or on deer’s pedicles , where their antlers grow and are shed, can attract these parasites. Once the eggs hatch, the maggots burrow into the animal’s flesh and feed, enlarging the wound and attracting more flies. Over time, this leads to infection and death. All warm-blooded animals are susceptible to the New World screwworm, but America has seen firsthand the harm they can cause to livestock. In the 1950s, livestock producers in the U.S. Southwest lost up to US$100 million annually to New World screwworm infections, equivalent to over $1 billion today. The nation was eventually able to eradicate the New World screwworm from the mainland in 1966 using a combination of treating infected animals and raising hundreds of millions of sterilized male flies and releasing them in infested areas. The New World screwworm has a life cycle of only about 21 days, and each female mates only once. Because of that, inundating areas with sterile male flies for a few months, which equates to a few generations of flies, can eradicate a screwworm population. Over time, sterile flies were used to push the New World screwworm further south, where they had been contained behind the Darién Gap , Panama’s narrow border region with Colombia. Sterile flies kept the parasite south of Panama for years, but the movement of cattle and wildlife likely brought it north again . Since 2022, the parasites have been reproducing and moving farther northward . There have been hundreds of detections in Mexico and now in the U.S. Wildlife have received far less attention than livestock during screwworm infestations, with one exception: In July 2016, the New World screwworm was detected in the Florida Keys in an endangered deer population : the Florida Key deer ( Odocoileus virginianus clavium ). At the time, the Florida Key deer population was estimated at only about 800 to 1,000 individuals . Because they were endangered and isolated, primarily on the islands of Big Pine Key and No Name Key , they were monitored more closely than most wildlife. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service biologists established quarantine zones. They inspected more than 16,900 animals – dogs, cats, a pig and a raccoon were also found with larvae – and they released 150 million sterile flies across the area. The islands lost 9% to 20% of the total Key Deer population , but the New World screwworm was declared eradicated there on March 23, 2017, less than a year after it was discovered. In June 2026, screwworm was back in the United States. A rancher discovered the first New World screwworm case in a calf near La Pryor, Texas. A few more cases were confirmed in livestock and domestic animals in Texas and New Mexico . The number of cases in animals had passed 120 as of Nov. 7, 2026 , including in two elk reported by hunters in Texas . The U.S. government has started ramping up production of sterile flies to try to keep the parasites from spreading. Although there have been only a couple of cases reported in wildlife, that isn’t necessarily reassuring. Wildlife are far more likely to carry the parasite without being detected. Once the screwworm is detected, treatment would also be much more complicated for wildlife than for livestock, because wildlife cannot be treated individually and thus are more dependent on the use of sterile flies to eradicate screwworm. For this reason, quickly identifying areas with New World screwworm and targeting those areas by releasing sterile flies would be more important than ever. Fortunately, there is an army of conservationists across the country who spend much of their time afield. These conservationists are also known as hunters. According to the latest U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service National Survey of Fishing, Hunting, and Wildlife-Associated Recreation, nearly 11.5 million hunters pursue big game and spend part of the fall and winter in the field hunting ungulate species such as deer and elk. White-tailed deer ( Odocoileus virginianus ) hunters alone are expected to harvest about 6 million deer during the 2026-27 season and will observe millions more. Hunters also review tens of millions of wildlife pictures collected each year by game cameras used for scouting. That level of surveillance can’t be matched. New Mexico’s Department of Agriculture has already called on hunters to report any suspicious larvae, particularly in Grant and Otero counties, where screwworm has been found in livestock. Hunters of all kinds, everywhere, can help. If you’re a hunter, be on the lookout for wounded animals , especially those with visible maggots, and for unusual behaviors such as restlessness, lethargy, or biting or licking wounds. Do not move harvested animals from the field if they show signs of a New World screwworm infection. Doing so could further spread the parasite. Instead, contact the area’s state wildlife agency , the U.S. Department of Agriculture office or a local veterinarian immediately. As hunting seasons get underway across the country, an army of conservationists will be in the field, and they have an important role to play in detecting and managing screwworm’s spread. Hunters already contribute to conservation through license fees, excise taxes and keeping wildlife populations at healthy densities. In the face of New World screwworm, their observations may be most valuable for protecting livestock. This article, originally published Nov. 6, 2026, has been updated with a rising number of cases.
